title: Lesson 5: Knowing When to Involve a Supervisor
summary: Not every disagreement needs management. Repeated problems, hostility, safety issues and serious misconduct should be escalated promptly and professionally.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Direct resolution, professional escalation and the CLEAR reporting method

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: A therapist notices that a colleague repeatedly fails to complete her assigned room-preparation duties. She raises the concern respectfully. The colleague apologises and promises to improve. However, the same problem continues.

The therapist becomes frustrated. Should she continue correcting her colleague every day? Should she argue with her? Should she discuss the issue with other employees? Or should she involve the supervisor?
The appropriate response may now be to involve the designated supervisor.
Knowing when to seek supervisory assistance is an important part of professional conflict resolution.
Not every disagreement requires management intervention. However, some situations cannot be resolved effectively through informal discussion alone.

sections.title: 2. What does involving a supervisor mean?
paragraphs: It means bringing a work-related concern to the attention of the person responsible for providing guidance, clarifying responsibilities, resolving disputes or taking appropriate action.
It should not be treated as an opportunity to punish someone personally.
The purpose is to obtain assistance with a genuine issue.

sections.title: 3. Situations employees may resolve directly
paragraphs: Some minor concerns can be addressed through respectful communication.
Example: "The towels weren't replenished after the last session. Please, can we ensure they're checked before the room is handed over?"
If the colleague acknowledges the issue and corrects it, supervisory intervention may not be necessary.
list: A colleague forgetting to replenish a shared item once.
A misunderstanding about an appointment time.
A disagreement about a routine task.

sections.title: 4. Situations that may require supervisory assistance

items.label: Repeated unresolved problems
items.body: A concern continues after reasonable attempts to address it.

items.label: Disputes about responsibilities
items.body: Employees cannot agree on who is responsible for a particular task.

items.label: Communication breakdown
items.body: A disagreement is becoming hostile or prevents effective cooperation.

items.label: Operational disruption
items.body: A conflict is affecting appointments, service quality or essential responsibilities.

items.label: Safety, harassment or serious misconduct
items.body: Concerns involving threats, unsafe practices, harassment or serious breaches should be escalated promptly.

sections.title: 5. When employees should not wait
paragraphs: Some situations should be reported immediately rather than handled through repeated informal conversations.
Where an immediate danger exists, employees should take appropriate steps to protect safety and obtain urgent assistance.
Do not delay reporting a serious issue merely because you want to avoid appearing confrontational.

sections.title: 6. Reporting a concern is not automatically gossip
paragraphs: The difference lies in purpose, accuracy and the recipient.
Gossip: "Let me tell you how irresponsible this therapist is."
Professional reporting: "The room-preparation checklist has been incomplete on three occasions this week. I've raised it directly, but the issue continues. Could you help clarify the process?"
The second statement provides specific information to someone who can address the concern.

sections.title: 7. How to report an issue professionally — the CLEAR method

items.label: L — List relevant facts
items.body: Provide dates, incidents or other information you know to be accurate.

items.label: E — Explain the impact
items.body: Describe how the issue affects work, clients or team cooperation.

items.label: A — Account for previous steps
items.body: Explain any reasonable attempt already made to resolve the issue, where appropriate.

items.label: R — Request guidance or action
items.body: Ask for clarification, intervention or another appropriate next step.

sections.title: 8. Example of professional escalation
paragraphs: "Good afternoon. I would like to raise a concern about the room handover. On three occasions this week, the supplies were not replenished before the next appointment. I've discussed the issue with the colleague involved, but it has continued. This is affecting preparation time. Please, could you help clarify the responsibilities and the expected handover procedure?"
This report is factual and solution-focused. It does not need to include insults or exaggerated accusations.

sections.title: 9. What if the supervisor is involved in the problem?
paragraphs: If an employee has a serious concern about her direct supervisor, she should use another appropriate management or reporting channel.
An employee should not be required to report serious misconduct solely to the person accused of it.

sections.title: 10. What supervisors should do after receiving a complaint
paragraphs: A supervisor should not automatically assume that the person who reports first is correct.
list: Protect confidentiality as far as reasonably possible.
Monitor whether the issue is resolved.
Avoid retaliation against employees who raise concerns in good faith.

sections.title: 11. Lesson 5 case study
paragraphs: Two therapists repeatedly argue about treatment-room handovers. They have attempted to resolve the disagreement directly, but the problem continues and is affecting appointments.
Expected lesson: Supervisory assistance should be sought when a genuine issue remains unresolved or begins affecting work.
list: Why should both employees avoid personal accusations?
What practical process might prevent recurrence?

sections.title: 12. Practical exercise: Escalate or resolve directly?
table: A colleague forgets to replenish towels once and corrects it immediately
A repeated handover problem continues after discussion
A client reports an immediate safety concern
Escalate promptly and protect the client
Two employees have a minor misunderstanding and resolve it respectfully
No further escalation may be necessary
An instruction conflicts with an essential safety procedure

remember: A responsible employee knows when to solve a problem directly and when to seek help. Reporting a genuine concern is not weakness or betrayal; it is part of protecting professional standards and teamwork.
